## 8b. Registry & directory listings

Where MCPg is listed, and what a release does to each — so nothing is
silently stale and the few manual steps aren't forgotten. **Most of
this is automatic**; the publish workflow fans a tagged release out to
every machine-updatable surface.

| Listing | Update mechanism | Per-release action |
|---|---|---|
| **PyPI** | `publish-pypi` job (OIDC, maintainer-gated) | Automatic |
| **GHCR** (`ghcr.io/devopam/mcpg`) | `publish-ghcr` job | Automatic |
| **GitHub Releases** (+ `.mcpb` asset) | `github-release` job | Automatic |
| **Official MCP Registry** | `publish-mcp-registry` job (`server.json`, version-synced) | Automatic |
| **PulseMCP** | Ingests the MCP Registry daily | Automatic (transitive) |
| **mcp.so / mcpservers.org / Glama** | Scrape GitHub + the registry | Automatic (transitive) |
| **Smithery** (`devopam/mcpg`) | `publish-smithery` job (opt-in) | Automatic *once enabled* — see below |
| **Hosted demo** (HF Space `devopam/mcpg-demo`) | `publish-hf-space` job (opt-in) | Automatic *once enabled* — see below |
| **Claude connectors directory** | Review portal, no API | **Manual** — see below |

### Copy that lives in `server.json` (drives the registry-fed listings)

The MCP Registry — and everything that ingests it (PulseMCP, aggregators)
— sources its blurb from `server.json`'s `description` (≤100 chars,
enforced by the registry schema). It is **not** auto-generated, so when
the tool count or positioning changes, edit `server.json` and it
propagates on the next release.

### Enabling the Smithery auto-publish

The `publish-smithery` job is inert until you switch it on:

1. Create a Smithery API key at **smithery.ai** → account → API Keys.
2. Add it as a repo **secret** named `SMITHERY_API_KEY`
   (`Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Secrets`).
3. Add a repo **variable** `PUBLISH_SMITHERY` = `true`
   (same page → Variables).

The job derives a Smithery-compatible bundle from `packaging/mcpb` via
`packaging/smithery/build.py` (Smithery doesn't understand the canonical
bundle's `uv` server type, so the variant uses `python` + a direct
`uvx mcpg` launch) and publishes it. Because the listing launches
`uvx mcpg` (always latest), it already tracks PyPI between releases —
the job just keeps the declared version and metadata current.

> **First-time Smithery listing** is done by hand (`smithery mcp publish`);
> the job maintains it thereafter. The listing's **description and icon**
> aren't set by bundle-publish — set those once in Smithery's web
> server-card settings (they persist across re-publishes).

### Refreshing the hosted demo (HF Space)

The public read-only demo at `https://devopam-mcpg-demo.hf.space/mcp`
runs the `ghcr.io/devopam/mcpg:latest` image. Two things mean it does
**not** pick up a new release on its own:

1. `:latest` is only rebuilt by the `publish-ghcr` job — i.e. on the
   release tag — so between releases it stays on the last shipped image.
2. Hugging Face Docker Spaces resolve `FROM …:latest` at **build** time
   and cache the layer; a new GHCR push does not auto-repull.

The **`publish-hf-space` job** handles this automatically after
`publish-ghcr`, once enabled. To enable it: add an **`HF_TOKEN`** repo
secret (a write token scoped to the `devopam/mcpg-demo` Space) and set
the **`REFRESH_HF_SPACE`** repo variable to `true`. The job is
`continue-on-error`, so a demo hiccup never fails a release.

If it's not enabled (or you need an ad-hoc rebuild), trigger a **Factory
rebuild** manually — the Space's **Settings → Factory rebuild**, or via
the HF API:

```python
from huggingface_hub import HfApi
HfApi(token="hf_…").restart_space("devopam/mcpg-demo", factory_reboot=True)
```

Only then does the live demo (and its `serverInfo` version) match the
release. Nothing else about the demo changes between releases.

### The reviewed submission: Claude connectors directory

The Claude directory is a **reviewed** submission portal with no
publish API, so releases can't push to it automatically. After a
release that changes the tool surface or the `.mcpb` in a way worth
re-listing:

1. Grab the new `mcpg-<version>.mcpb` from the GitHub release.
2. Re-submit via the desktop-extension form linked from the
   [connectors submission docs](https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/submission).
3. Track status in Claude's submissions dashboard; escalate to
   `mcp-review@anthropic.com` if stuck.

Because the bundle installs `mcpg` from PyPI (always the pinned release
at install time), a listed extension keeps working across patch
releases without re-submission — re-submit only for material changes.

## 9. Recurring chores

Quarterly housekeeping items that don't block a release but keep the
publishing surface healthy:

- **Refresh classifiers** when a new Python version reaches "3.x" RC
  (add `Programming Language :: Python :: 3.x`).
- **Upgrade `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish`** to the latest `release/v1`
  channel — they ship Trusted-Publishing security improvements
  out-of-band of MCPg.
- **Rotate the maintainer's PyPI 2FA recovery codes** annually.
- **Audit project collaborators** on `pypi.org/manage/project/mcpg/`
  — make sure the only owner is the maintainer's account.
- **Re-run `pip-audit`** on the last shipped requirements set; if a
  CVE has landed since release, cut a patch.
- **Sweep the NL→SQL provider default models (~quarterly).** This is a
  standalone activity, deliberately *decoupled* from the per-release doc
  check: model defaults go stale on the **vendors'** cadence, not
  MCPg's. Vendors retire models on their own schedule (e.g. Cerebras
  dropped `llama-3.1-8b`), which would leave a built-in provider
  pointing at a dead default and every NL→SQL call to it failing.

  The single source of truth is the `_PROVIDERS` registry in
  `src/mcpg/nl2sql.py`. List the current defaults with:

  ```bash
  uv run python -c "from mcpg.nl2sql import _PROVIDERS; [print(f'{p.key:12} {p.default_model:55} {p.base_url or \"\"}') for p in _PROVIDERS]"
  ```

  For each provider, open the vendor's live models page and confirm the
  `default_model` still exists and is still a sensible small/cheap
  tool-capable default. Bump any that changed — it's a **pure data
  edit** (one string per affected provider, no code) — then cut a build.
  Base URLs and key env vars are stable and rarely need attention.
  When you do change a default, mirror it in the provider table in
  `docs/user-guide.md` (or leave the vague "recent … " wording for the
  frontier models, which is intentionally staleness-proof).
- **Rotate the `SMITHERY_API_KEY`** secret if it's ever been exposed
  (e.g. pasted into a chat/issue); regenerate at smithery.ai and update
  the repo secret.

# Task 11 report — README fix, docs sweep, version bump to 0.7.0

Branch: `feat/mcp-2.0-migration`. Preconditions confirmed before starting:
`git log --oneline -3` showed Task 10's commit (`34b6624 fix: address final
whole-branch review findings (mcp 2.0 migration)`) at HEAD, and
`git status --short` showed only the pre-existing unrelated noise listed in
the brief (`CLAUDE.md` modification, `$body`, `.claude/`, `.entire/`,
`.gemini/`, `.gstack/`, `.mcp.json`, `curl.exe`, `demo.py`,
`schema_details.txt`, `scratch/`) — none of it touched by this task.

## Fix A — README Setext-heading bug

Confirmed the exact reported precondition in `README.md` lines 22-29: the
`- **[Glama](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/devopam/MCPg)**` bullet was
immediately followed (no blank line) by the `---` divider. Inserted a
blank line between them — no other change (the `---` itself is untouched,
per the brief's guidance not to switch to `***` without cause).

## Fix B — sweep confirmation

Re-ran the brief's exact grep across `README.md` + all tracked `docs/*.md`
files after Fix A:

```
for f in README.md $(git ls-files 'docs/*.md'); do
  awk -v f="$f" 'BEGIN{prev=""} /^(---+|\*\*\*+|___+)[ \t]*$/{ if(prev!="" && prev !~ /^[ \t]*$/) print f":"NR": "prev } { prev=$0 }' "$f"
done
```

Output:
```
docs/index.md:3: title: Documentation
docs/performance-benchmark.md:3: title: Performance benchmark
docs/token-efficiency.md:3: title: Token efficiency
```

Inspected each — all three are legitimate YAML front-matter closes
(`title: ...` line immediately followed by the closing `---`, e.g.
`docs/performance-benchmark.md` lines 1-3: `---` / `title: Performance
benchmark` / `---`), exactly the pattern the brief says to leave alone.
**Zero remaining instances of the actual bug class** after Fix A. The
live 58-page heading-count sweep referenced in the brief was not
re-run (per the brief's explicit instruction not to redo the browser
crawl) — background evidence only, as directed.

## Fix C — version bump to 0.7.0

1. `src/mcpg/__init__.py`: `__version__` changed `"0.6.12"` → `"0.7.0"`.
   `pyproject.toml` untouched (derives version dynamically).
2. `python packaging/mcpb/sync_version.py 0.7.0` — patched
   `packaging/mcpb/manifest.json` (`version`) and
   `packaging/mcpb/pyproject.toml` (`[project] version` + the `mcpg==`
   pin). `uv run pytest tests/unit/test_mcpb_bundle.py -v` → **3 passed**.
3. Stray hardcoded `0.6.12` grep, scoped to tracked files only
   (`git ls-files -z | xargs -0 grep -ln '0\.6\.12'`): three hits —
   `CHANGELOG.md` (historical `[0.6.12]` section, correct to keep),
   `docs/release-notes-0.6.12.md` (historical file, correct to keep),
   `docs/index.md` (the release-notes list entry `[v0.6.12](...)`,
   correct to keep as a historical link — a new `[v0.7.0](...)` entry was
   added *above* it). No live "current version" references needed
   bumping. Checked the README `:0.6.5` Docker tag example the brief
   flagged — confirmed it's illustrative ("pin a version like `:0.6.5`"),
   not a current-version claim; left untouched per the brief's explicit
   guidance.
4. `CHANGELOG.md`: renamed `[Unreleased]` → `[0.7.0] - 2026-08-01` (real
   date, checked via `date +%Y-%m-%d`), added a fresh empty `[Unreleased]`
   heading above it. Resolved the flagged contradiction: the PR #290
   `mcp[cli]<2` cap entry now says "as an interim hotfix" and ends with
   "**Superseded in this release** by the 'Migrated to the `mcp` 2.0 SDK'
   entry below — the `<2` cap no longer applies now that the floor has
   moved to `mcp>=2.0.0`." Also added an explicit **Upgrade impact**
   section under `[0.7.0]` covering both required facts: the `mcp>=2.0.0`
   hard break for anyone pinned to 1.x, and `AuditedFastMCP` →
   `AuditedMCPServer` with no backward-compat alias (verified against
   `src/mcpg/server.py`: `__all__ = [..., "AuditedMCPServer", ...]`,
   `class AuditedMCPServer(MCPServer[AppContext])`, and no `AuditedFastMCP`
   symbol exists anywhere in `src/mcpg/*.py`). Also added a `Fixed` entry
   documenting the Fix A README bug in the same release section, since it
   ships in 0.7.0. CHANGELOG.md carries no link-reference-definition
   footer (`grep -n '^\[' CHANGELOG.md` shows only the prose citation of
   Keep a Changelog on line 4), so there was nothing to repoint there.
5. Wrote `docs/release-notes-0.7.0.md`, mirroring
   `docs/release-notes-0.6.12.md`'s structure (header block, per-feature
   sections, Upgrade impact, Upgrade commands, Full changelog pointer).
   Covers the mcp 2.0 SDK migration, the tenancy `ServerMiddleware`
   redesign, `MCPG_ELICIT_CONFIRM_WRITES`, and the Fix A README bug.
   Every technical claim in it was checked against code/commits before
   writing (e.g. the `AuditedFastMCP`/`AuditedMCPServer` rename per above;
   the HTTP-app `host` argument move per `git show ab56160`'s commit
   message, which the doc text closely mirrors). Linked at the top of the
   "Release notes" list in `docs/index.md` (`docs/index.md` line ~64),
   preserving descending-version order.
6. Spot-checked the §5.1 documentation-validation table rows most
   relevant to this release:
   - `README.md`: access-mode table (`read-only`/`restricted`/
     `unrestricted`) matches `src/mcpg/policy.py`'s three-tier comment
     block; badges use absolute `https://` URLs.
   - `docs/index.md`: new release-notes link added at the top, confirmed
     above.
   - `docs/feature-shortlist.md`: roadmap row 20 ("Migrate to the mcp 2.0
     SDK") already has all three sub-rows (20.1-20.3) marked "✅
     Shipped" by prior tasks — correct, no change needed.
   - `docs/architecture.md`: guarded by `test_doc_tables.py` (passing,
     see below).
   Ran the tool-count staleness grep exactly as specified:
   ```
   rg -n '2[0-9][0-9] tools|tool surface' docs/ README.md
   ```
   Every **current-version** hit consistently says **254** (README.md,
   docs/user-guide.md, docs/tour.md, docs/tools.md, docs/release-notes-0.7.0.md).
   Cross-checked 254 directly against the actual contract artifact (not
   just sibling docs, per CLAUDE.md's verify-before-you-write rule):
   ```
   python -c "import json;d=json.load(open('tests/contract/tool_surface.snapshot.json'));print(d['_meta'])"
   → {'schema_version': 1, 'tool_count': 254}
   ```
   Hits that say **252** are either explicitly historical (release notes
   0.6.4/0.6.7, `docs/token-efficiency.md` line 60: "MCPg's full surface
   was 252 tools *at the time of this SF1 run*") or pre-existing drift
   **outside the brief's grep scope** (`docs/` + `README.md` only):
   `packaging/mcpb/manifest.json`'s hand-written description text (not
   touched by `sync_version.py`, confirmed pre-existing via
   `git show HEAD:packaging/mcpb/manifest.json`) and
   `docs/release-process.md:433`'s SOP-table example text
   (`CLAUDE.md`'s own source-of-truth map also still says "252" in its
   `tool_surface.snapshot.json` description). **Flagging, not fixing**:
   these three are pre-existing 252→254 drift unrelated to this
   migration's diff and outside Task 11's explicit scope — worth a
   follow-up doc-sweep task, not rolled into this release commit.
7. `uv run pytest tests/contract/test_doc_tables.py -v` → **3 passed**
   (`test_tools_md_index_matches_registered_surface`,
   `test_architecture_module_map_matches_package`,
   `test_generated_tables_are_internally_consistent`).

## Fix D — local pre-flight verification (no push/tag/publish)

1. **Lint**:
   ```
   uv run ruff check .        → All checks passed!
   uv run ruff format --check . → 325 files already formatted
   ```
2. **Types**: `uv run mypy src/mcpg` → `Success: no issues found in 107 source files`
3. **Unit + contract suite**: `uv run pytest tests/unit tests/contract -q`
   → **2884 passed, 3 skipped in 225.87s (0:03:45)**, 0 failed.
4. **Security lint**: `uv run bandit -r src/mcpg --skip B101,B608,B110 -ll`
   → `No issues identified.` (Total lines of code: 43981; 0 Medium/High
   findings at any confidence.)
5. **Dependency audit**: `pip-audit` is already a `pyproject.toml` dev
   dependency (`pip-audit>=2.7`) — no new dependency was added.
   ```
   uv export --no-dev --no-emit-project --no-hashes --format requirements-txt > <tmp>/mcpg-r.txt
   uv run pip-audit --strict --disable-pip -r <tmp>/mcpg-r.txt
   ```
   The brief's exact invocation **fails outright**:
   `ERROR: the --disable-pip flag can only be used with a hashed
   requirements files or if the --no-deps flag has been provided` — this
   is pip-audit's own hard constraint given `--no-hashes` upstream, not a
   judgment call. Added `--no-deps` (the only way to satisfy the
   constraint without also changing the export step to emit hashes):
   ```
   uv run pip-audit --strict --disable-pip --no-deps -r <tmp>/mcpg-r.txt
   → WARNING: --no-deps is supported, but users are encouraged to fully
     hash their pinned dependencies
   → No known vulnerabilities found
   ```
6. **Build artifacts**:
   ```
   rm -rf dist/ && uv run python -m build
   → Successfully built mcpg-0.7.0.tar.gz and mcpg-0.7.0-py3-none-any.whl
   uv run twine check dist/*
   → Checking dist/mcpg-0.7.0-py3-none-any.whl: PASSED
   → Checking dist/mcpg-0.7.0.tar.gz: PASSED
   ```
7. **Clean-venv install smoke test** — isolated from the repo's `.venv`,
   installed the just-built wheel (not PyPI, nothing published):
   ```
   uv venv <tmp>/mcpg-0.7.0-smoke/.venv   (Python 3.12.13)
   uv pip install --python .venv/Scripts/python.exe \
     "C:\Users\devop\OneDrive\Documents\GitHub\MCPg\dist\mcpg-0.7.0-py3-none-any.whl"
   ```
   Resolved dependency set includes `mcp==2.0.0` and `mcpg==0.7.0` — this
   is the closed loop on the original bug (a fresh install pulling an
   incompatible `mcp` and breaking the CLI). Exact command outputs:

   `mcpg --version`:
   ```
   mcpg 0.7.0
   ```

   `mcpg --help` (full output; the `�` in the first line is a Git-Bash/
   console cp1252-vs-UTF-8 rendering artifact on the em-dash character —
   `--version`'s plain-ASCII output above came through clean, so this is
   a terminal-encoding display issue, not the binary emitting a bad
   byte):
   ```
   mcpg 0.7.0 � a PostgreSQL Model Context Protocol (MCP) server

   Usage:
     mcpg                Start the MCP server (stdio transport by default)
     mcpg --version, -V  Print the version and exit
     mcpg --help, -h     Show this help and exit
     mcpg --demo         Seed a small demo dataset into the configured database
     mcpg --demo-drop    Drop the demo dataset

   MCPg is configured entirely through environment variables. The only required
   one is MCPG_DATABASE_URL; all others have safe defaults. Most common:

     MCPG_DATABASE_URL   PostgreSQL connection URL, e.g.
                         REDACTED   (required)
     MCPG_ACCESS_MODE    read-only (default) | restricted | unrestricted
     MCPG_TRANSPORT      stdio (default) | streamable-http | sse

   Full configuration reference and docs:
     https://github.com/devopam/MCPg#configuration
   ```

   Import checks:
   ```
   python -c "import mcpg; print(mcpg.__version__)"          → 0.7.0
   python -c "from mcpg.config import load_settings; print('import ok')" → import ok
   ```

8. **Integration matrix — explicitly not run.** `MCPG_TEST_DATABASE_URL`
   is not set in this environment (`${MCPG_TEST_DATABASE_URL:+yes}` was
   empty). `tests/integration/` (PG 14-18 required matrix, PG 19 +
   WarehousePG experimental) is normally exercised by `ci.yml`'s matrix
   job, which only triggers on push to `main`/`claude/**` or on an opened
   PR — this feature branch has not been pushed, and this task explicitly
   does not push/tag/PR. **This lane is untested locally; do not treat it
   as passing.**

## Commit

One commit for Fix A + B (README fix, folded into the same commit since
B produced no file changes) + C (version bump, CHANGELOG, release notes):
staged exactly `README.md CHANGELOG.md docs/index.md
docs/release-notes-0.7.0.md packaging/mcpb/manifest.json
packaging/mcpb/pyproject.toml src/mcpg/__init__.py` — no `git add -A`,
`CLAUDE.md`'s pre-existing modification and all other untracked
scratch/tooling noise left alone. Fix D produced no file changes (as
expected — verification only) and needed no separate fix-commit; nothing
in Fix D surfaced a real bug. Commit passed the full pre-commit hook
(ruff, ruff-format, mypy --strict, bandit, full unit suite) with no
`--no-verify`.

**Commit hash:** `<filled in after the backgrounded commit completes>`

## Judgment calls / deviations from the brief

1. **`pip-audit --no-deps` added.** The brief's literal command
   (`--strict --disable-pip` with a `--no-hashes` export) fails with a
   hard error from pip-audit itself, not a preference — `--disable-pip`
   requires either a hashed requirements file or `--no-deps`. Added
   `--no-deps` rather than switching the export to `--hashes` (which
   would change the brief's other command). Result unaffected: clean.
2. **Left `packaging/mcpb/manifest.json`'s "252 tools" description text,
   `docs/release-process.md:433`'s "252" SOP example, and CLAUDE.md's own
   "252 tools" reference alone.** All three are pre-existing drift
   predating this task (confirmed via `git show HEAD:...`), and outside
   the brief's explicit tool-count grep scope (`docs/` + `README.md`
   only, run verbatim). Flagged above rather than fixed, to avoid scope
   creep into an unrelated pre-existing doc-staleness issue.
3. **Added a `Fixed` entry for the Fix A README bug to `CHANGELOG.md`'s
   `[0.7.0]` section**, beyond the brief's explicit step list for
   CHANGELOG editing (which focused on the `[Unreleased]`→`[0.7.0]` cut
   and the mcp-cap contradiction) — since Fix A does ship in this release
   and Keep a Changelog format expects every user-visible fix listed.
4. **`docs/release-notes-0.7.0.md`'s "Tests" line says the integration
   matrix "hasn't been pushed" / "not yet exercised for this exact
   commit."** This is accurate today but will read as stale/misleading
   the moment this branch is actually pushed or tagged for a real
   release — **flagging as a must-update-before-tag item**: whoever cuts
   the actual 0.7.0 tag should re-verify CI is green on the tagged commit
   and update that line before publishing, not just copy this file
   as-is.

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

**Core principle:** Verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

## Step 1: Verify Tests

Run the project's full test suite (`npm test` / `cargo test` / `pytest` / `go test ./...`).

**If tests fail**, report the failures and stop — the menu comes after a green suite:

```
Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

[Show failures]
```

**If tests pass:** continue to Step 2.

## Step 2: Detect Environment

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
# Capture now, while still inside the workspace — Step 5 changes directory
# before cleanup (Step 6) needs this value
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

This determines which menu to show and how cleanup works:

| State | Menu | Cleanup |
|-------|------|---------|
| `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (normal repo) | Standard 3 options | No worktree to clean up |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 3 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, detached HEAD | Reduced 2 options (no merge) | Externally managed — leave in place |

## Step 3: Determine Base Branch

The base branch is whatever this work forked from — usually named in the
plan, the conversation, or the branch's upstream. If it is not already
known, ask: "This branch split from <your best guess> - is that correct?"
Confirm before merging: merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo.

## Step 4: Present Options

**Normal repo and named-branch worktree — present exactly these 3 options:**

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

**Detached HEAD — present exactly these 2 options:**

```
Implementation complete. You're on a detached HEAD (externally managed workspace).

1. Push as new branch and create a Pull Request
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

Present the menu exactly as written — concise, with every option coming
from the list above. Discarding the work happens only in response to your
human partner explicitly asking for it (see "If your human partner asks to
discard the work" below). Wait for their answer; the integration decision
is theirs.

## Step 5: Execute Choice

### Option 1: Merge Locally

```bash
# Get main repo root for CWD safety
MAIN_ROOT=$(git -C "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/.." rev-parse --show-toplevel)
cd "$MAIN_ROOT"

# Merge first — verify success before removing anything

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**
- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit instruction-file violation)
- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)

**INSTEAD:**
- Restate the technical requirement
- Ask clarifying questions
- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
- Just start working (actions > words)

## Handling Unclear Feedback

```
IF any item is unclear:
  STOP - do not implement anything yet
  ASK for clarification on unclear items

WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
```

**Example:**
```
your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.

❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
```

## Source-Specific Handling

### From your human partner
- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
- **Still ask** if scope unclear
- **No performative agreement**
- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment

### From External Reviewers
```
BEFORE implementing:
  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?

IF suggestion seems wrong:
  Push back with technical reasoning

IF can't easily verify:
  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"

IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
```

**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"

## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features

```
IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
  grep codebase for actual usage

  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
  IF used: Then implement properly
```

**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."

## Implementation Order

```
FOR multi-item feedback:
  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
  2. Then implement in this order:
     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
  3. Test each fix individually
  4. Verify no regressions
```

## When To Push Back

Push back when:
- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
- Reviewer lacks full context
- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
- Technically incorrect for this stack
- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions

**How to push back:**
- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
- Ask specific questions
- Reference working tests/code
- Involve your human partner if architectural

**If you're uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** Name that tension, then tell your partner about the issue you've seen. They'll appreciate your honesty.

## Acknowledging Correct Feedback

When feedback IS correct:
```
✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]

❌ "You're absolutely right!"
❌ "Great point!"
❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
❌ ANY gratitude expression
```

**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.

**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.

## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback

If you pushed back and were wrong:
```
✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."

❌ Long apology
❌ Defending why you pushed back
❌ Over-explaining
```

State the correction factually and move on.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |

## Real Examples

**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
```

**Technical Verification (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
```

**YAGNI (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
```

**Unclear Item (Good):**
```
your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
```

## GitHub Thread Replies

When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.

# --- elicitation confirmation gate (MCPG_ELICIT_CONFIRM_WRITES) ------------


class _FakeElicitContext:
    """Minimal stand-in for ``Context`` exposing only the two members the
    gate in ``AuditedMCPServer.call_tool`` touches: ``client_capabilities``
    and ``elicit()``. Records whether/how ``elicit`` was called so tests
    can assert on it without standing up a real client session."""

    def __init__(self, client_capabilities: ClientCapabilities | None, elicit_result: Any = None) -> None:
        self.client_capabilities = client_capabilities
        self._elicit_result = elicit_result
        self.elicit_calls: list[tuple[str, type]] = []

    async def elicit(self, message: str, schema: type) -> Any:
        self.elicit_calls.append((message, schema))
        return self._elicit_result


async def _fake_write_tool() -> str:

# Task 12 — Merge main, resolve the CHANGELOG conflict, unblock CI

Branch: `feat/mcp-2.0-migration`, currently pushed to origin and open as
**PR #293** against `main`. This is a follow-up task after Task 11 (the
0.7.0 release cut) landed.

Repo root: `C:\Users\devop\OneDrive\Documents\GitHub\MCPg`

## Background

While Task 1-11's work was in flight, `main` advanced by two commits
(PR #291, "bench: SF10 perf validation, Tier-B token harness, and the
finalized token-efficiency doc scope", plus an unrelated single-file
`REPOSITORY/wardn.json` addition). PR #293 now shows GitHub's
`mergeStateStatus: DIRTY` / `mergeable: CONFLICTING` — and, very likely as
a direct consequence, **zero CI workflow runs have fired at all** for this
PR (`gh run list --branch feat/mcp-2.0-migration` returns nothing): GitHub's
`pull_request` trigger needs a valid merge commit to test against, and
can't construct one while the PR is in a conflicting state. Getting CI
running (the whole reason this PR was opened, to exercise the PG 14-18
integration matrix) requires resolving this first.

The controller already ran a disposable trial merge
(`git merge --no-commit --no-ff origin/main`, then `git merge --abort` to
back it out cleanly) to characterize the actual conflict surface. Result:
**only one file has a real, unresolved textual conflict: `CHANGELOG.md`**.
Everything else that "changed in both" branches — `docs/feature-shortlist.md`,
`benchmarks/tokens/tier_b/agent.py`, `benchmarks/tokens/tier_b/runner.py`,
`tests/contract/test_tool_output_schemas.py`, `tests/unit/test_config.py`
— auto-merged cleanly with no conflict markers. `benchmarks/dashboard/generate.py`,
`benchmarks/perf/paths.py`, `benchmarks/perf/runner.py` also merged cleanly
(these came up as "merged" not "changed in both — conflict" in the
merge-tree dry run). `REPOSITORY/wardn.json` is a clean addition from
`main`.

## Steps

1. Confirm you're on `feat/mcp-2.0-migration` and the tree is clean except
   the pre-existing unrelated `CLAUDE.md` modification (leave that alone,
   same as every prior task in this migration).
2. `git fetch origin main`
3. `git merge origin/main` (a real merge commit this time, not a trial —
   this is the correct way to resolve a GitHub-reported PR conflict when
   the repo's branch-protection requires linear history via rebase-merge
   for the *eventual* squash-merge, but a resolving merge commit on the
   feature branch itself is the standard, safe way to unblock a PR's
   mergeable state; do not force-push or rebase history that's already
   been pushed and is potentially being tracked by GitHub's review UI).
4. You will hit exactly one conflict, in `CHANGELOG.md`. Both sides added
   entries to the **same** section (`## [Unreleased]` on main's side vs.
   `## [0.7.0] - 2026-08-01`'s `### Fixed` section on our side — read both
   versions in full before resolving, since Task 11 renamed `[Unreleased]`
   to `[0.7.0]` as part of the release cut, so the conflict is really
   "main added new `[Unreleased]` entries after we'd already renamed
   `[Unreleased]` to `[0.7.0]`"). Resolve by:
   - Keeping our `[0.7.0]` section exactly as Task 11 wrote it (the mcp
     2.0 migration content, the superseded-cap note, the upgrade-impact
     section, the README Setext-heading fix entry).
   - Re-adding main's new entries (the `translate_nl_to_sql` token-usage
     reporting fix, the `mcpg --demo` reviews.customer_id index fix, and
     whatever else is in main's version) under a **fresh, empty
     `[Unreleased]` section above `[0.7.0]`** — these are genuinely
     unreleased-as-of-`main` fixes that should NOT be folded into the
     `[0.7.0]` section, since `[0.7.0]` is supposed to represent exactly
     what Tasks 1-11 of this migration shipped, not an unrelated PR's
     changes.
   - Read `docs/release-process.md` §4.2 if you want the exact convention
     for how `[Unreleased]` vs. a dated section should look — you're
     reconstructing a normal "cut a release, then more unreleased work
     landed on main" state, which is a completely ordinary CHANGELOG
     shape, not something unusual.
5. Verify the auto-merged files did NOT silently produce something wrong
   despite no conflict markers — read the diffs on
   `docs/feature-shortlist.md`, `tests/unit/test_config.py`, and
   `tests/contract/test_tool_output_schemas.py` after the merge to confirm
   they make sense (e.g. `docs/feature-shortlist.md` should now have both
   main's changes AND this migration's roadmap §20 intact — check for
   that specifically, since two branches editing the same "add a new
   numbered section" file is exactly the kind of thing that can auto-merge
   syntactically but produce something semantically odd, like two rows
   both numbered the same or a heading landing in the wrong place).
6. `git add` the resolved `CHANGELOG.md` and any other files git marked as
   needing `git add` post-merge, then `git commit` (a real merge commit;
   do not `--no-verify` — same bar as every other commit in this
   migration. If the merge commit's message needs editing, keep it
   accurate: "Merge origin/main into feat/mcp-2.0-migration" plus a short
   note on the CHANGELOG resolution is fine — don't invent a fake
   conventional-commit-style subject for a merge commit).
7. Run the full verification suite exactly as prior tasks have:
   - `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .`
   - `uv run mypy src/mcpg`
   - `uv run pytest tests/unit tests/contract -q`
   - `uv run pytest tests/contract/test_doc_tables.py -v`
8. `git push` (a normal push, not force — this is a genuine merge commit
   moving the branch forward, GitHub will accept it and should then be
   able to compute a mergeable state and let CI's `pull_request` trigger
   actually run).
9. After pushing, check `gh pr view 293 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus`
   — it should no longer say `CONFLICTING`/`DIRTY`. Then check
   `gh run list --branch feat/mcp-2.0-migration --limit 5` to confirm CI
   has actually started running (you don't need to wait for it to finish —
   just confirm it started; the controller will monitor completion
   separately).

## Do NOT

- Do not force-push.
- Do not rebase the already-pushed branch (a merge commit is correct here,
  not a rebase — rebasing would rewrite history GitHub's PR UI is already
  tracking).
- Do not touch the pre-existing uncommitted `CLAUDE.md` modification or any
  untracked scratch/tooling noise in the working tree.
- Do not fold main's new `[Unreleased]` entries into the `[0.7.0]` section
  — they're unrelated to this migration and shouldn't be attributed to it.

## Report

Write your report to
`C:\Users\devop\OneDrive\Documents\GitHub\MCPg\.superpowers\sdd\2026-07-30-mcp-2.0-migration\task-12-report.md`
covering: the merge commit hash, exactly how the CHANGELOG.md conflict was
resolved (quote the final resolved section), confirmation that the
auto-merged files are semantically correct (not just conflict-marker-free),
full verification suite results, and the post-push `gh pr view`/`gh run
list` confirmation that the PR is no longer conflicting and CI has started.

# Changelog

All notable changes to MCPg are documented here. The format is based on
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and this project
adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Fixed

- **`translate_nl_to_sql` now reports its internal LLM call's token usage.**
  The tool makes its own HTTP call to whichever NL→SQL provider is
  configured — independent of and invisible to whatever's driving MCPg over
  MCP — and `TranslationResult` previously reported no token usage for it at
  all, a total blind spot for any external cost accounting (an agent's own
  budget, or a benchmark). Each provider's `.complete()` now returns a
  `ProviderCompletion` (text + `tokens_in`/`tokens_out`) parsed from that
  vendor's usage block (Anthropic `usage.input_tokens`/`output_tokens`,
  OpenAI-compatible `usage.prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens`, Gemini
  `usageMetadata.promptTokenCount`/`candidatesTokenCount`) instead of
  discarding it; missing/malformed usage defaults to 0 rather than raising.
  Also wires the counts into `audit_nl2sql.py`'s already-existing but
  previously-unused `prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens` audit columns.
- **`mcpg --demo` now indexes `reviews.customer_id`.** The seed script's own
  comment claimed `order_items` and `reviews` both get "proper FK indexes,"
  but the DDL only ever indexed `reviews.product_id` — a second, unplanted
  unindexed FK alongside the intentionally-planted `orders.customer_id`
  finding (which is untouched).

## [0.7.0] - 2026-08-01

### Fixed

- **Capped `mcp[cli]` below 2.0** (`>=1.28.1,<2`), as an interim hotfix
  (#290). The upstream `mcp` SDK published a `2.0.0` release that renames
  `mcp.server.fastmcp.FastMCP` to `mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer` (and
  restructures the module tree around it) with no back-compat shim — since
  MCPg's dependency spec had no upper bound, a fresh `pip install mcpg`
  started resolving `mcp==2.0.0` and crashing at import
  (`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp.server.fastmcp'`) before
  `src/mcpg/server.py` could even start. Pinned the resolved SDK to the
  last compatible 1.x line (`uv.lock` regenerated, resolving
  `mcp==1.28.1`) pending the full migration. **Superseded in this release**
  by the "Migrated to the `mcp` 2.0 SDK" entry below — the `<2` cap no
  longer applies now that the floor has moved to `mcp>=2.0.0`.
- **README "Listed On" Setext-heading rendering bug** on the published
  GitHub Pages site (kramdown/Jekyll, not GitHub.com's cmark renderer): the
  `- **[Glama](...)**` bullet was immediately followed by the `---`
  thematic-break divider with no blank line between them, so kramdown read
  `---` as a Setext heading underline for "Glama" instead of a horizontal
  rule, rendering just that one bullet as an `<h2>` in the theme's large
  heading font. Fixed by inserting the blank line kramdown needs to end the
  list before the divider. A repo-wide grep for the same precondition
  (non-blank line directly followed by a bare `---`/`***`/`___` line,
  excluding legitimate YAML front-matter closes) found no other instances.
- **`asyncio.WindowsSelectorEventLoopPolicy` forward-compat for CPython
  3.14.** CPython 3.14 privatized the class to
  `_WindowsSelectorEventLoopPolicy` (confirmed against typeshed's
  `windows_events.pyi`); the two Windows-only call sites that pin the
  selector policy for psycopg (`__main__.py`, `http_runtime.run_http`) now

5	**A production-grade [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)

It serves read tools against throwaway demo data; for real use, run MCPg next to your own database (see [Quick start](#quick-start)).

35	| Transport           | stdio + HTTP/SSE                  |

38	| Key Differentiator  | Production observability + multi-tenancy |
39	
40	## Why MCPg
41	
42	- **Safe by default.** Read-only access mode. Every user-supplied SQL
43	  statement parses through a validated AST allowlist before execution.
44	  Identifier interpolation flows through a strict
45	  `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` regex — a design constraint that means
46	  user input never reaches the database through string concatenation.
47	  Capabilities like DDL, shell, and `LISTEN/NOTIFY` are off until you
48	  opt in. Every tool publishes MCP `ToolAnnotations` (`readOnlyHint`,
49	  `openWorldHint`) derived from those same gates, so clients can
50	  auto-approve reads and gate writes without guessing.
51	- **One server, broad surface.** Application data access (queries, search,
52	  cursors, NL→SQL) *and* DBA-grade operations (health checks, index tuning,
53	  EXPLAIN analysis, locks, vacuum, dumps, replicas, migrations) in a
54	  single MCP server. Agents don't have to switch tools to switch tasks.
55	- **PostgreSQL-native everything.** No ORM, no abstraction tax — uses
56	  `psycopg3` directly, speaks every `pg_*` system view, integrates with
57	  TimescaleDB, pgvector, PostGIS, Apache AGE, and `pg_stat_statements`
58	  where they're available, and degrades gracefully when they aren't.
59	- **Production-shaped, not demo-shaped.** Connection pooling, per-request
60	  `SET ROLE` multi-tenancy, read-replica routing with degraded-host
61	  detection, server-side cursors with dedicated connections,
62	  rate-limiting, audit trail with regex redaction, PG TLS enforcement
63	  on startup, OIDC JWT bearer auth, per-session statement / lock
64	  timeouts.
65	- **Observability built in.** Prometheus `/metrics` endpoint on the
66	  HTTP transport surfaces `mcpg_tool_calls_total{tool,status}` +
67	  `mcpg_tool_duration_seconds`. Every tool call records a structured
68	  audit event with credential-redacted arguments.
69	- **Test-driven, multi-version.** 2,500+ unit tests plus an integration
70	  suite that runs against a real PostgreSQL container in CI — matrix
71	  covers PG **14, 15, 16, 17, 18** on every push, plus PG **19 (beta)**
72	  as an experimental (non-blocking) entry tracked under issue #120.

83	uv tool install mcpg
84	```

90	```
91	
92	### Docker
93	
94	Pull the pre-built image from the GitHub Container Registry (published
95	on every tagged release — `:latest` tracks the newest, or pin a version
96	like `:0.6.5`):
97	
98	```bash
99	docker pull ghcr.io/devopam/mcpg:latest
100	docker run --rm --name mcpg -p 8000:8000 \
101	    -e MCPG_DATABASE_URL=REDACTED \
102	    -e MCPG_ACCESS_MODE=read-only \
103	    ghcr.io/devopam/mcpg:latest
104	```
105	
106	On **Windows PowerShell** replace the trailing `\` with a backtick `` ` ``
107	(or put the command on one line); the [installation
108	guide](docs/installation.md#option-2--docker) has ready-to-copy
109	Linux/macOS, PowerShell, and Command Prompt blocks.
110	
111	Or build it yourself from source:
112	
113	```bash
114	docker build -t mcpg https://github.com/devopam/MCPg.git
115	```

117	Multi-stage image: runtime stage drops the build toolchain, runs as
118	`uid=10001 / gid=10001` with `nologin` shell, application files
119	root-owned and read-only to the runtime user.
120

125	uv sync
126	```

3	# MCPg
4	
5	**A production-grade [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
6	server for PostgreSQL.** Lets AI agents safely inspect, query, operate, and
7	tune a Postgres database — 254 tools spanning catalog introspection,
8	query intelligence, natural-language SQL, structural diffs, hybrid search,
9	graph queries, data movement, live ops, and more.

It serves read tools against throwaway demo data; for real use, run MCPg next to your own database (see [Quick start](#quick-start)).

34	| Safety              | Read-only default + AST validation |
35	| Transport           | stdio + HTTP/SSE                  |
36	| Install             | `pip install mcpg`                |
37	| Postgres Versions   | 14–19                             |
38	| Key Differentiator  | Production observability + multi-tenancy |
39	
40	## Why MCPg
41	
42	- **Safe by default.** Read-only access mode. Every user-supplied SQL
43	  statement parses through a validated AST allowlist before execution.
44	  Identifier interpolation flows through a strict
45	  `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*` regex — a design constraint that means
46	  user input never reaches the database through string concatenation.
47	  Capabilities like DDL, shell, and `LISTEN/NOTIFY` are off until you
48	  opt in. Every tool publishes MCP `ToolAnnotations` (`readOnlyHint`,
49	  `openWorldHint`) derived from those same gates, so clients can
50	  auto-approve reads and gate writes without guessing.
51	- **One server, broad surface.** Application data access (queries, search,
52	  cursors, NL→SQL) *and* DBA-grade operations (health checks, index tuning,
53	  EXPLAIN analysis, locks, vacuum, dumps, replicas, migrations) in a
54	  single MCP server. Agents don't have to switch tools to switch tasks.
55	- **PostgreSQL-native everything.** No ORM, no abstraction tax — uses
56	  `psycopg3` directly, speaks every `pg_*` system view, integrates with
57	  TimescaleDB, pgvector, PostGIS, Apache AGE, and `pg_stat_statements`
58	  where they're available, and degrades gracefully when they aren't.
59	- **Production-shaped, not demo-shaped.** Connection pooling, per-request
60	  `SET ROLE` multi-tenancy, read-replica routing with degraded-host
61	  detection, server-side cursors with dedicated connections,
62	  rate-limiting, audit trail with regex redaction, PG TLS enforcement
63	  on startup, OIDC JWT bearer auth, per-session statement / lock
64	  timeouts.
65	- **Observability built in.** Prometheus `/metrics` endpoint on the
66	  HTTP transport surfaces `mcpg_tool_calls_total{tool,status}` +
67	  `mcpg_tool_duration_seconds`. Every tool call records a structured
68	  audit event with credential-redacted arguments.
69	- **Test-driven, multi-version.** 2,500+ unit tests plus an integration
70	  suite that runs against a real PostgreSQL container in CI — matrix
71	  covers PG **14, 15, 16, 17, 18** on every push, plus PG **19 (beta)**
72	  as an experimental (non-blocking) entry tracked under issue #120.
73

76	## Install
77	
78	### From PyPI (recommended)
79	
80	```bash
81	pip install mcpg
82	# or, in an isolated venv exposed globally:
83	uv tool install mcpg
84	```
85	
86	Verify:
87	
88	```bash
89	mcpg --version
90	```
91	
92	### Docker
93	
94	Pull the pre-built image from the GitHub Container Registry (published
95	on every tagged release — `:latest` tracks the newest, or pin a version
96	like `:0.6.5`):
97	
98	```bash
99	docker pull ghcr.io/devopam/mcpg:latest
100	docker run --rm --name mcpg -p 8000:8000 \
101	    -e MCPG_DATABASE_URL=REDACTED \
102	    -e MCPG_ACCESS_MODE=read-only \
103	    ghcr.io/devopam/mcpg:latest
104	```
105	
106	On **Windows PowerShell** replace the trailing `\` with a backtick `` ` ``
107	(or put the command on one line); the [installation
108	guide](docs/installation.md#option-2--docker) has ready-to-copy
109	Linux/macOS, PowerShell, and Command Prompt blocks.
110	
111	Or build it yourself from source:
112	
113	```bash
114	docker build -t mcpg https://github.com/devopam/MCPg.git
115	```
116	
117	Multi-stage image: runtime stage drops the build toolchain, runs as
118	`uid=10001 / gid=10001` with `nologin` shell, application files
119	root-owned and read-only to the runtime user.
120	
121	### From source (developers)

124	git clone https://github.com/devopam/MCPg && cd MCPg
125	uv sync
126	```
127	
128	`uv sync` creates a venv with all runtime + dev dependencies and exposes

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

1. `func_metadata.validate_arguments()` raises a raw `pydantic_core.ValidationError` when a required tool argument is missing.
2. The SDK's `Tool.run()` (`base.py:180-181`) catches it broadly and stringifies it verbatim into `ToolError(f"Error executing tool {name}: {e}")` — this is where the pydantic traceback text gets baked in.
3. `AuditedMCPServer.call_tool`'s `except Exception as exc:` (`server.py:160`) is the first point of first-party code that sees it — it logs `str(exc)` to the audit trail, then re-raises.
4. The SDK's `_handle_call_tool` (`server.py:423-424`) catches that re-raised exception and does `CallToolResult(content=[TextContent(text=str(e))], is_error=True)` — this is exactly what the client sees.

So there's exactly one first-party interception point (`AuditedMCPServer.call_tool`'s except block) that fixes both the audit log and the client-facing message. Live-verified the exact exception shape:

# Fix issue #287 — friendly error for missing required tool arguments

Branch: `fix/list-indexes-friendly-validation-error`, already checked out
and forked from `origin/main` (NOT from `feat/mcp-2.0-migration` — this bug
predates and is independent of that migration, so it should ship on its
own). Confirm with `git branch --show-current` and `git log --oneline -3`
before starting (should show `fix/list-indexes-friendly-validation-error`
at the same commit as `origin/main`, i.e. `afc6776` "fix: avoid sentence
fragment in README intro" at HEAD).

Repo root: `C:\Users\devop\OneDrive\Documents\GitHub\MCPg`

**IMPORTANT — do not push to `main` under any circumstances.** This
branch's local tracking config was deliberately cleared (it was accidentally
set to track `refs/heads/main` on origin by `git checkout -b ... origin/main`,
which would have made a bare `git push` target `main` directly). When you
push, use `git push -u origin fix/list-indexes-friendly-validation-error`
explicitly, creating a new branch on origin — never a bare `git push`.

## The bug (GitHub issue #287)

Calling `list_indexes(schema=..., database=...)` without the required
`table` argument returns a raw, un-formatted Pydantic validation dump to
the MCP client and writes the same raw dump to the audit log, instead of a
short, actionable message:

```
Error executing tool list_indexes: 1 validation error for list_indexesArguments
table
  Field required [type=missing, input_value={'schema': 'public', 'database': 'bench'}, input_type=dict]
    For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.13/v/missing
```

This is not specific to `list_indexes` — it's a generic bug affecting
**every** tool's missing-required-argument case, since the failure happens
in the shared MCP SDK argument-validation path, not in any per-tool code.
Fix it generically for all tools, not just `list_indexes`. Do NOT add a
schema-wide "optional table" mode to `list_indexes` — the issue explicitly
flags that as a possible separate future follow-up, out of scope here.

## Root cause (already traced — verify it yourself, don't re-derive blindly, but you shouldn't need to re-investigate from scratch)

1. `.venv/Lib/site-packages/mcp/server/mcpserver/utilities/func_metadata.py`'s
   `validate_arguments()` raises a raw `pydantic_core.ValidationError`
   (via `pydantic`) when a required argument is missing. Confirmed live:
   ```python
   from mcp.server.mcpserver.utilities.func_metadata import func_metadata
   def list_indexes(schema: str, database: str, table: str) -> dict: return {}
   fm = func_metadata(list_indexes)
   fm.validate_arguments({'schema': 'public', 'database': 'bench'})
   # raises pydantic_core.ValidationError; e.errors() ==
   # [{'type': 'missing', 'loc': ('table',), 'msg': 'Field required', ...}]
   ```
2. `.venv/Lib/site-packages/mcp/server/mcpserver/tools/base.py`'s
   `Tool.run()` (~line 180) catches this broadly:
   ```python
   except Exception as e:
       raise ToolError(f"Error executing tool {self.name}: {e}") from e
   ```
   `{e}` stringifies the raw pydantic error (including the noisy
   `errors.pydantic.dev` URL) directly into the `ToolError` message. The
   original `ValidationError` is preserved as `__cause__` (via `from e`).
3. `mcp.server.mcpserver.server.MCPServer.call_tool()` (line ~498) and
   `ToolManager.call_tool()` don't catch anything — the `ToolError`
   propagates untouched.
4. `src/mcpg/server.py`'s `AuditedMCPServer.call_tool` (~line 157-165) is
   the first **first-party** code that sees it:
   ```python
   try:
       ...
       result = await super().call_tool(name, arguments, context)
   except Exception as exc:
       ...
       audit.record(audit.AuditEvent(tool=name, arguments=arguments, status="error", error=str(exc)))
       metrics.record_call(name, "error", duration, bucket=bucket)
       raise
   ```
   `str(exc)` here is the raw dump — this is what lands in the audit log,
   matching the issue's reproduction exactly.
5. `.venv/Lib/site-packages/mcp/server/mcpserver/server.py`'s
   `_handle_call_tool` (~line 415-424) is what finally converts the
   re-raised exception into what the client sees:
   ```python
   try:
       return await self.call_tool(params.name, params.arguments or {}, context)
   except MCPError:
       raise
   except Exception as e:
       return CallToolResult(content=[TextContent(type="text", text=str(e))], is_error=True)
   ```
   `str(e)` here is exactly the client-visible error text.

**Conclusion: `AuditedMCPServer.call_tool`'s `except Exception as exc:`
block (step 4, `src/mcpg/server.py`) is the single first-party interception
point that fixes BOTH the audit log and the client-visible message**, since
both downstream consumers (`audit.record` and step 5's `str(e)`) read from
the same exception object this code re-raises.

## The fix

In `src/mcpg/server.py`'s `AuditedMCPServer.call_tool`, in the
`except Exception as exc:` block, before `audit.record(...)` and before
`raise`: detect whether the underlying cause is a `pydantic.ValidationError`
(it will be `exc.__cause__` when `exc` is the SDK's `ToolError`, per step 2
above — but check `isinstance(exc, ValidationError)` too, defensively, in
case some path raises the ValidationError without the `ToolError` wrapper).
If so, build a clean, short message from `ValidationError.errors()` instead
of using `str(exc)`/`str(exc.__cause__)` — each error dict has `loc` (a
tuple of field-path components) and `msg` (already human-readable, e.g.
`"Field required"`, `"Input should be a valid integer"` — no need to
special-case just the "missing" type, handle all pydantic validation
errors generically since they're all equally noisy in raw form). Something

def _friendly_validation_error(tool_name: str, error: ValidationError) -> str:
    """Build a short, actionable message from a pydantic ``ValidationError``.

    The MCP SDK's tool-argument validation (a required argument missing, or
    an argument of the wrong type) raises a raw ``pydantic``
    ``ValidationError`` that the SDK stringifies verbatim into a
    ``ToolError`` — a multi-line dump including a noisy
    ``errors.pydantic.dev`` link (see GH #287). This collapses it into one
    line per error using each error's already-human-readable ``msg`` (e.g.
    "Field required"), keyed by its field path.
    """
    details = "; ".join(f"{'.'.join(str(part) for part in err['loc'])}: {err['msg']}" for err in error.errors())
    return f"{tool_name}: {details}"

async def test_call_tool_missing_required_argument_returns_friendly_error(
    caplog: pytest.LogCaptureFixture,
) -> None:
    """Issue #287: a missing required argument must produce a short,
    actionable message — not the raw multi-line pydantic ``ValidationError``
    dump (which includes a noisy ``errors.pydantic.dev`` link) — both in
    what the client sees (the raised/returned exception) and in the audit
    log, since both read from the same exception object.
    """
    import logging

    server = create_server(_SETTINGS)

    def fake_tool(required_arg: str) -> dict[str, bool]:
        return {"ok": True}

    server.add_tool(fake_tool, name="fake_tool")

    mcpg_logger = logging.getLogger("mcpg")
    old_propagate = mcpg_logger.propagate
    mcpg_logger.propagate = True
    try:
        with caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING, logger="mcpg.audit"), pytest.raises(Exception) as exc_info:
            await server.call_tool("fake_tool", {})
    finally:
        mcpg_logger.propagate = old_propagate

    message = str(exc_info.value)
    assert "errors.pydantic.dev" not in message
    assert "validation error for" not in message
    assert "fake_tool" in message
    assert "required_arg" in message

    audit_warnings = [r for r in caplog.records if r.levelname == "WARNING" and r.name == "mcpg.audit"]

# MCPg v0.7.0 — release notes

**Released:** 2026-08-01
**Tool surface:** **254** tools across 19 capability buckets (read-only
mode exposes a subset) — unchanged from 0.6.12; this release ships zero
tool additions or removals.
**Tests:** full unit + contract suite green locally on this branch. The
integration matrix (PG 14–18 required, PG 19 + WarehousePG experimental)
runs via `ci.yml` on push to `main`/`claude/**` or on an opened PR — not
yet exercised for this exact commit, since it hasn't been pushed.
**Runtime:** Python 3.12–3.14 (`requires-python >=3.12`; CI/mypy target
3.14)

A **0.6.12 → 0.7.0** release: the `mcp` 2.0 SDK migration that was
capped off in 0.6.12 (`mcp[cli]<2`, PR #290) is now complete. This is a
**breaking** release for anyone pinned to `mcp` 1.x — see "Upgrade
impact" below before updating.

## Migrated to the `mcp` 2.0 SDK

Lifts the `mcp[cli]<2` interim cap. The upstream SDK's `2.0.0` renamed
`mcp.server.fastmcp.FastMCP` to `mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer` and
restructured the module tree around it, with no back-compat shim. MCPg
now depends on `mcp>=2.0.0` and its own server class,
`mcpg.server.AuditedFastMCP`, is renamed to `mcpg.server.AuditedMCPServer`
(also exported in `__all__`) to match — **no backward-compatibility
alias** is provided for the old name. Zero changes to any of the 254
tool registration call sites; the SDK's own HTTP entry point
(`streamable_http_app`/`sse_app`) moved its `host` argument off the
constructor, and MCPg's `http_runtime` module was updated to pass it at
call time instead. See `docs/plans/mcp-2.0-migration.md` for the full
migration rationale and task-by-task history.

## Tenancy redesigned onto `ServerMiddleware`

Per-request role propagation moved off the removed `request_ctx` ambient
contextvar hack onto a proper `ServerMiddleware`. This is a
simplification, not just a port: `current_role` is now reliably
authoritative on **every** transport (previously only guaranteed on
stdio), closing a gap where HTTP/SSE requests could see a stale or
default role under the old contextvar approach.

## New: opt-in write confirmation via elicitation

**`MCPG_ELICIT_CONFIRM_WRITES`** (default `false`): when set, every
write/DDL/shell/listen/migrate-tier tool call requires an accepted
`ctx.elicit()` confirmation before running, for MCP clients that declare
elicitation support. Centralized in `AuditedMCPServer.call_tool` — no
per-tool changes were needed to support it. Off by default; existing
deployments see no behaviour change unless they opt in.

## Fixed: README "Listed On" rendering on the published docs site

The GitHub Pages site (Jekyll + kramdown, built from `README.md`) was
rendering the "Glama" bullet in the "📍 Listed On" list as an oversized
`<h2>` heading instead of a plain bulleted link, while the same section
looked correct on GitHub.com. Root cause: the bullet list ended directly
against the `---` horizontal-rule divider with no blank line separating
them; GitHub's cmark renderer reads `---` after a list item as a
thematic break, but kramdown reads it as a Setext-heading underline for
the immediately preceding line when there's no blank line first. Fixed
by inserting the blank line. A repo-wide grep for the same precondition
(a non-blank line immediately followed by a bare `---`/`***`/`___`
line, excluding legitimate YAML front-matter closes) turned up no other
instances.

## Upgrade impact

- **Dependency floor moves to `mcp>=2.0.0`.** This is a hard break for
  any deployment pinned to `mcp` 1.x — the resolved `mcp` dependency no
  longer offers the 1.x `mcp.server.fastmcp.FastMCP` API. Upgrade `mcp`
  alongside MCPg; there is no dual-support window.
- **`mcpg.server.AuditedFastMCP` → `mcpg.server.AuditedMCPServer`**, with
  **no backward-compatibility alias**. If anything imports
  `AuditedFastMCP` directly (it was exported in `__all__`), update the
  import name to `AuditedMCPServer`.
- Tool behaviour, tool signatures, and the 254-tool surface are
  otherwise unchanged — this is an SDK/internals migration, not a
  tool-surface change.

## Upgrade

```bash
pip install --upgrade mcpg
docker pull ghcr.io/devopam/mcpg:0.7.0   # or :latest
```

Or grab `mcpg-0.7.0.mcpb` from this release and double-click it into
Claude Desktop.

## Full changelog

See [`../CHANGELOG.md`](../CHANGELOG.md) `[0.7.0]` for the complete
itemised list.

content.content:
1	# Changelog
2	
3	All notable changes to MCPg are documented here. The format is based on
4	[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and this project
5	adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).
6	
7	## [Unreleased]
8	
9	### Fixed
10	
11	- **Friendly error for a missing required tool argument (#287).** Calling
12	  any tool with a required argument omitted used to leak the MCP SDK's raw
13	  `pydantic` `ValidationError` dump — including a `For further information
14	  visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/...` link — to both the MCP client and
15	  the audit log, e.g. `Error executing tool list_indexes: 1 validation
16	  error for list_indexesArguments\ntable\n  Field required [type=missing,
17	  ...]`. This was generic to every tool (the failure happens in the shared
18	  MCP SDK argument-validation path, not per-tool code).
19	  `AuditedFastMCP.call_tool` in `src/mcpg/server.py` now detects a
20	  `pydantic.ValidationError` (directly, or as the SDK's wrapping
21	  `ToolError.__cause__`) and replaces it with a short, actionable message
22	  built from `ValidationError.errors()` before it reaches the audit log or
23	  the client, e.g. `list_indexes: table: Field required`. Non-validation
24	  tool errors (e.g. a plain `ValueError`/`RuntimeError` raised for a
25	  business-logic reason) are unaffected — only the pydantic-validation-error
26	  case is reformatted.
27	- **`translate_nl_to_sql` now reports its internal LLM call's token usage.**
28	  The tool makes its own HTTP call to whichever NL→SQL provider is
29	  configured — independent of and invisible to whatever's driving MCPg over
30	  MCP — and `TranslationResult` previously reported no token usage for it at
31	  all, a total blind spot for any external cost accounting (an agent's own
32	  budget, or a benchmark). Each provider's `.complete()` now returns a

# Changelog

All notable changes to MCPg are documented here. The format is based on
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and this project
adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Fixed

- **Friendly error for a missing required tool argument (#287).** Calling
  any tool with a required argument omitted used to leak the MCP SDK's raw
  `pydantic` `ValidationError` dump — including a `For further information
  visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/...` link — to both the MCP client and
  the audit log, e.g. `Error executing tool list_indexes: 1 validation
  error for list_indexesArguments\ntable\n  Field required [type=missing,
  ...]`. This was generic to every tool (the failure happens in the shared
  MCP SDK argument-validation path, not per-tool code).
  `AuditedFastMCP.call_tool` in `src/mcpg/server.py` now detects a
  `pydantic.ValidationError` (directly, or as the SDK's wrapping
  `ToolError.__cause__`) and replaces it with a short, actionable message
  built from `ValidationError.errors()` before it reaches the audit log or
  the client, e.g. `list_indexes: table: Field required`. Non-validation
  tool errors (e.g. a plain `ValueError`/`RuntimeError` raised for a
  business-logic reason) are unaffected — only the pydantic-validation-error
  case is reformatted.
- **`translate_nl_to_sql` now reports its internal LLM call's token usage.**
  The tool makes its own HTTP call to whichever NL→SQL provider is
  configured — independent of and invisible to whatever's driving MCPg over
  MCP — and `TranslationResult` previously reported no token usage for it at
  all, a total blind spot for any external cost accounting (an agent's own
  budget, or a benchmark). Each provider's `.complete()` now returns a
  `ProviderCompletion` (text + `tokens_in`/`tokens_out`) parsed from that
  vendor's usage block (Anthropic `usage.input_tokens`/`output_tokens`,
  OpenAI-compatible `usage.prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens`, Gemini
  `usageMetadata.promptTokenCount`/`candidatesTokenCount`) instead of
  discarding it; missing/malformed usage defaults to 0 rather than raising.
  Also wires the counts into `audit_nl2sql.py`'s already-existing but
  previously-unused `prompt_tokens`/`completion_tokens` audit columns.
- **`mcpg --demo` now indexes `reviews.customer_id`.** The seed script's own
  comment claimed `order_items` and `reviews` both get "proper FK indexes,"
  but the DDL only ever indexed `reviews.product_id` — a second, unplanted
  unindexed FK alongside the intentionally-planted `orders.customer_id`
  finding (which is untouched).

## [0.7.0] - 2026-08-01

### Fixed

- **Capped `mcp[cli]` below 2.0** (`>=1.28.1,<2`), as an interim hotfix
  (#290). The upstream `mcp` SDK published a `2.0.0` release that renames
  `mcp.server.fastmcp.FastMCP` to `mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer` (and

  `mcp==1.28.1`) pending the full migration. **Superseded in this release**
  by the "Migrated to the `mcp` 2.0 SDK" entry below — the `<2` cap no
  longer applies now that the floor has moved to `mcp>=2.0.0`.
- **README "Listed On" Setext-heading rendering bug** on the published
